ican: I can explain the Doppler effect in terms of wavefronts.
I can state whether fo is higher or lower, and justify it.
I can state that the Doppler effect also shifts light.

cloze.title: Say it the exam way
cloze.text:
A sound source moves towards an observer. The wavefronts in front of it are [[closer together|further apart]]. The observer hears a [[higher|lower]] frequency.

The source then moves away. The wavefronts behind it are [[further apart|closer together]], so [[fewer|more]] wavefronts reach the observer each second. The frequency heard is [[lower|higher]]. The frequency of the source itself [[does not change|changes]].

This is the [[Doppler|Hubble]] effect. It causes shifts in the wavelengths of sound and of light. For a source moving towards the observer, the bottom of the fraction is [[v − vₛ|v + vₛ]].

warmup_mc.alt: A buzzer travels at constant speed as it approaches, passes and moves away from a stationary observer. It emits sound of constant frequency. The frequency heard: A remains constant, B continually decreases, C continually increases, D changes from a low frequency to a high frequency, E changes from a high frequency to a low frequency.
fb: Not this one. The buzzer's own frequency stays the same, but the frequency heard does not. Think about the wavefronts in front of the buzzer and behind it.
Not this one. The frequency heard does not keep falling. It is higher while the buzzer comes towards the observer and lower while it moves away. It drops as the buzzer passes.
Not this one. Moving away spreads the wavefronts out, so the frequency heard goes down, not up.
Not this one. That is the wrong way round. Coming towards you squashes the wavefronts together, so the first sound is the higher one.
Right. Coming towards the observer, the wavefronts are closer together, so the frequency heard is higher. Moving away, they are further apart, so it is lower.

mc.alt: A siren on an ambulance emits sound at a constant frequency of 750 Hz. The ambulance travels at a constant speed of 25.0 metres per second towards a stationary observer. The speed of sound in air is 340 metres per second. The frequency heard by the observer is: A 695 Hz, B 699 Hz, C 750 Hz, D 805 Hz, E 810 Hz.
fb: Not this one. This has the fraction upside down, so the answer is lower than 750 Hz. The ambulance is coming towards the observer, so the frequency heard is higher.
Not this one. This uses <var>v</var> + <var>v</var><sub>s</sub>, the sign for a source moving away. This ambulance is coming towards the observer.
Not this one. 750 Hz is the siren's own frequency. The ambulance is moving, so the observer hears a different frequency.

Not this one. This multiplies by (<var>v</var> + <var>v</var><sub>s</sub>) ÷ <var>v</var>. Use the relationship on the data sheet: <var>f</var><sub>o</sub> = <var>f</var><sub>s</sub> × <var>v</var> ÷ (<var>v</var> − <var>v</var><sub>s</sub>).

mc.alt: A car horn emits a sound with a constant frequency of 405 Hz. The car travels away from a student at 28.0 metres per second. The speed of sound in air is 335 metres per second. The frequency heard by the student is: A 371 Hz, B 374 Hz, C 405 Hz, D 439 Hz, E 442 Hz.
fb: Not this one. This has the fraction upside down and uses <var>v</var> − <var>v</var><sub>s</sub>, the sign for a source coming towards you. Use <var>f</var><sub>o</sub> = <var>f</var><sub>s</sub> × <var>v</var> ÷ (<var>v</var> + <var>v</var><sub>s</sub>) for a source moving away.
Not this one. 405 Hz is the horn's own frequency. The car is moving, so the student hears a different frequency.

Not this one. This has the fraction upside down: it multiplies by (<var>v</var> + <var>v</var><sub>s</sub>) ÷ <var>v</var>. Use the relationship on the data sheet: <var>f</var><sub>o</sub> = <var>f</var><sub>s</sub> × <var>v</var> ÷ (<var>v</var> + <var>v</var><sub>s</sub>).
Not this one. This uses <var>v</var> − <var>v</var><sub>s</sub>, the sign for a source coming towards you. This car is moving away.

paper2.alt: Ultrasound from a probe reflects from red blood cells moving along a blood vessel, at angle theta to the direction of blood flow. The change in frequency is given by delta f = 2 f v cos theta divided by v, where v sub rbc is the velocity of the red blood cells. The transmitted frequency is 3.70 megahertz, the velocity of the ultrasound is 1540 metres per second, the angle is 60.0 degrees and the change in frequency is 286 hertz. Calculate the velocity of the red blood cells. 2 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2019 Paper 2 Question 5(b): 1 mark for substituting 286 = 2 × 3.70 × 10⁶ × v cos 60.0 ÷ 1540, and 1 mark for v = 0.119 metres per second. Also accepted: 0.12, 0.1190, 0.11904.

paper2.alt: A train travels at constant speed towards a bridge. A horn on the train emits sound of frequency 270 Hz. A person on the bridge hears 290 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 metres per second. Part (b)(ii): the train passes under the bridge. Explain why the frequency heard by the person on the bridge decreases as the train passes under the bridge and then moves away. You may wish to use a diagram. 1 mark.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2017 Section 2 Question 1(b)(ii), 1 mark: fewer wavefronts per second, or the wavefronts are further apart, or the wavelength increases, or a diagram with wavefronts closer together ahead of the train and further apart behind it. A diagram must show the direction of travel. Not accepted: any answer that says the frequency or wavelength of the horn itself changes.
